solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Spot about to be covered by ointment

indicators.note: the word for 'about' sits under a covering of the ointment word, so it goes inside it

parts.note: a lotion is a soothing ointment
CA, short for circa, means about

explanation.surface: A blemish that needs dabbing with cream.
explanation.definitionFit: A spot is a place or site, the sense of the noun 'location'.

clue.text: Some mountaineers resolve to climb? They're not successful

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means the letters read upwards, backwards
some takes a portion of the letters across the two words

explanation.surface: Climbers determined to scale peaks who fail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to climb' reverses the run of letters found in 'mountaineers resolve'.
explanation.definitionFit: People who fail to win are those that lose; plural noun matches plural definition.

clue.text: Throw up a lot after Canadian melon

indicators.note: the scrambled letters follow the Canadian abbreviation

parts.note: CAN is the abbreviation for Canadian

indicators.note: to throw is to disorder or upset, so the letters of the phrase are scrambled

explanation.surface: Vomiting heavily after eating a Canadian melon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throw up' reads as vomit; 'Throw' alone rearranges UPALOT into TALOUP.
explanation.definitionFit: A cantaloup is a variety of musk melon with orange flesh; example of melon.

clue.text: Slow run around yard

indicators.note: around is read as moving the letters about, rearranging the run word and the yard letter

parts.note: to dart is to run quickly

explanation.surface: Jogging sluggishly around the back yard.
explanation.walkthrough: A flawed clue: 'around' must shuffle DART plus Y, an indirect anagram. Reading it as DART reversed gives TRADY, not a word; the blog calls it a setter's slip.
explanation.definitionFit: Tardy means late or sluggish, the same as slow in arriving.

clue.text: Aida perhaps put on tie regularly for work

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece is placed on top of the other

parts.note: Aida is a Verdi opera, so an example of the genre

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of the word tie

explanation.surface: Getting dressed up in a tie to go to the opera.
explanation.definitionFit: To operate is to function or run, the verb work in that sense.

clue.text: Succeeded with cries to get strokes

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for succeeded, as in family trees
weeps means cries

explanation.surface: Someone wins, cries for joy, and is then caressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweeps are long strokes, as of a brush or an oar.

clue.text: They turn poorly within months after gale

indicators.note: the month portion comes after the gale word

parts.note: a gale is a strong wind

indicators.note: the poorly word goes inside the months abbreviation

parts.note: MS is an abbreviation for months
poorly means ill

explanation.surface: Someone falls sick for months after a storm.
explanation.definitionFit: Windmill sails rotate in the breeze, so these structures are things that turn.

clue.text: Queen wearing each large uniform

indicators.note: the each abbreviation wraps round the queen letters like clothing

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for large, as in clothing sizes

explanation.surface: The Queen dressed in matching large uniforms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uniform' looks like clothing the Queen is wearing; it is the adjective meaning even.
explanation.definitionFit: Uniform means the same throughout, i.e. even or identical in amount.

clue.text: Lashing out from son anticipated

parts.note: pending means about to happen, anticipated

explanation.surface: A son's predicted outburst of temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lashing out' suggests violence; it means splashing money about.
explanation.definitionFit: To lash out can mean to spend money freely; idiom.

clue.text: Small drawers containing Romeo's miscellaneous things

indicators.note: the underwear word holds the Romeo letter within it

parts.note: drawers are knickers, informally undies
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A tiny pair of knickers belonging to Shakespeare's lover, among odds and ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawers' looks like chests of drawers but means underpants.
explanation.definitionFit: Sundries are odds and ends, assorted small items not worth listing separately.

clue.text: Bear dying by river

parts.note: an end is a death, so dying gives the noun for one's finish
the Ure is a river in North Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A bear expiring on a riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' looks like the animal; it is the verb, to put up with.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear something is to tolerate or withstand it; synonym.

clue.text: Mistreated sailor's going to be employed

indicators.note: the sailor is going away, removed from the longer word

parts.note: abused means mistreated
AB, able seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: An ill-treated sailor about to be taken on.
explanation.definitionFit: Something employed has been put to use; synonym.

clue.text: Prepared to study by taking out book

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it at university

indicators.note: the book letter is removed from the little word 'by'

explanation.surface: Getting ready for an exam by pulling a book off the shelf.
explanation.definitionFit: Prepared and ready are synonyms: all set to act.

clue.text: See lambs — about 500 — flocked together

indicators.note: about signals the letters of the first two words being turned around into a new order

parts.note: D is 500 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Look at around five hundred lambs gathered in a flock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges SEELAMBS into ASSEMBLE; 'about 500' reads as an approximate count but D is simply added.
explanation.definitionFit: To assemble is to gather in one place, just as a flock gathers.

clue.text: Topping for smooth crumpet?

parts.note: crumpet is old slang for the head, and a smooth one is bald; the covering for it is a hairpiece

explanation.walkthrough: 'Crumpet' suggests the tea-time griddle cake with a topping like butter; here it is the head. Crumpet is a British teacake.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairpiece worn on top of a bald head is literally a topping for it.

clue.text: Handles old clubs including irons? On the contrary

indicators.note: including signals one piece placed within another
the reverse of what is written: the irons hold the old clubs, not the other way round

parts.note: to iron is to press, so irons means presses
C is the abbreviation for clubs, the card suit

explanation.surface: Golf: someone handles old clubs, irons among them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'irons' and 'clubs' suggest golf, but irons are pressing and clubs a card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: To process is to handle or deal with something methodically; synonym.

clue.text: DPhil with no struggling? One's intelligent, apparently

indicators.note: the letters of the degree and the little word are thrashing about into a new order

explanation.surface: A doctorate holder who never had to struggle must be clever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'struggling' rearranges DPHIL and NO; DPhil is Oxford's doctorate.
explanation.definitionFit: The marine mammal is reputed to be one of the most intelligent animals, hence 'apparently'.

clue.text: Waited, excited to embrace model

indicators.note: the excited word wraps its arms round the model word

parts.note: heated means excited or agitated
to sit for an artist is to model

explanation.surface: Someone waited, thrilled at hugging a model.
explanation.definitionFit: To hesitate is to pause before acting, i.e. to wait.

clue.text: Uninteresting aims — they won't get you anywhere

parts.note: dead can mean dull, lacking any activity
ends means aims or goals

explanation.surface: Dull ambitions lead nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Cul-de-sacs lead nowhere, and figuratively nor do fruitless lines of enquiry.

clue.text: Former policeman initially expected to get angry

parts.note: ex means former
Plod is British slang for a police officer, after Mr Plod in Noddy

indicators.note: initially takes just the opening letter of the word expected

explanation.surface: An ex-officer was predictably going to lose their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: PLOD is a slangy British name for a police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: To explode is to burst out in a fit of rage; idiom for getting angry.

clue.text: Ecstasy then retreat for old PM

parts.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy
a den is a private retreat

explanation.surface: A former Prime Minister taking ecstasy then going into hiding.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Eden was UK Prime Minister from 1955 to 1957.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Eden was a British Prime Minister in the 1950s; the clue names him by his office.

clue.text: Help from a relative in street

indicators.note: the relative is placed inside the street abbreviation

parts.note: sis, short for sister, is a relative

explanation.surface: Getting help from a family member who lives on your road.
explanation.definitionFit: To assist is to help; simple synonym.

clue.text: Try a lure, pursuing last of trout

indicators.note: the lure word chases, coming after, the fish letter
last of takes the final letter of the fish's name

parts.note: to tempt is to lure

explanation.surface: Fishing: casting a lure after a trout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lure' reads as fishing tackle; it is the verb tempt.
explanation.definitionFit: A try and an attempt are both an effort at something.

clue.text: Tense with dread at sea — getting flogged

parts.note: T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

indicators.note: at sea means confused, so the letters of dread are jumbled

explanation.surface: A sailor, tense with dread, about to be whipped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flogged' suggests whipping; it is British slang for sold.
explanation.definitionFit: To flog something is British slang for selling it, so traded matches.

clue.text: New doctor fired, entertaining fine hospital department

indicators.note: entertaining means holding as a guest, so the reworked letters take in the fine letter
to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters of fired are rearranged

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencils
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department

explanation.surface: A new doctor sacked while running a hospital department well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' looks like part of the story but is the definition; 'doctor' is the anagram verb turning FIRED into DIFER.
explanation.definitionFit: Something new is unlike what went before, i.e. novel or unfamiliar.

clue.text: Not as many sheep in France

indicators.note: the sheep is placed inside the France abbreviation

parts.note: a ewe is a female sheep

explanation.surface: France has fewer sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: Fewer means a smaller number of, the comparative of few.

clue.text: Phil ate Roger's sandwiches afterwards

indicators.note: the phrase holds the answer between its words like a filling in bread

explanation.surface: Phil ate Roger's sandwiches and was found out afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sandwiches' looks like food Phil ate; it is the verb saying the answer is held in the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Later and afterwards both mean at a subsequent time.

clue.text: Ladies almost set free

parts.note: the Ladies is the women's toilet, a loo

indicators.note: almost drops the final letter of the word set

explanation.surface: Women nearly let go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ladies' means a women's lavatory, a loo in British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose means not confined, at liberty; synonym of free.

clue.text: Most recent newts moving around Fink-Nottle's back

indicators.note: the rearranged amphibians go round the single letter
moving shifts the letters of newts into a new order
back gives the final letter of the name

explanation.surface: Gussie Fink-Nottle's latest newts crawling over him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' turns NEWTS into NEWST, which goes 'around' E. Gussie Fink-Nottle is P.G. Wodehouse's newt-fancier.
explanation.definitionFit: Newest is the superlative of new, meaning the most recent.

clue.text: Brought in minute drink — editor's after one

indicators.note: the earlier pieces come after the one, which leads

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: A quick drink, with the editor arriving after one o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: Imported goods are brought in from abroad.

clue.text: Anxiety as adult's lost hair

indicators.note: the adult letter is lost from the little word as

parts.note: A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: Worry as a grown-up sees their hair falling out.
explanation.definitionFit: Stress is mental strain or worry; synonym of anxiety.

clue.text: Took part in a bike race and finished

parts.note: the TT is the Isle of Man Tourist Trophy motorcycle race
ended means finished

explanation.surface: Joining a motorcycle race and completing it.
explanation.walkthrough: The TT is a famous motorbike race held on the Isle of Man.
explanation.definitionFit: To attend an event is to be present at it, taking part.
